images.caption: Figure 1:ImageNet samples with correction.Without the use of guidance, our correction method can achieve high-quality class-conditional (top) andunconditional(bottom) image samples.

Figure 2:Denoising and prediction correction.During training, the denoiser and corrector predict the same clean target. Stop-gradient blocks the correction loss through the denoiser’s prediction. During sampling, each denoising prediction is refinedKKtimes before the next sampling step.

Figure 3:Prediction correction improves structural coherence during sampling.We show clean-sample predictions𝒙^\hat{\bm{x}}along denoising trajectories without (a) and with (b) correction. In (a), early structural errors persist as later denoising steps add details. In (b), iterative correction revises the prediction at eachtt, producing more coherent object structures before the next denoising step. Each triplet shows this refinement within one denoising step. Additional visualizations are shown in AppendixD.2(Fig.36).

Figure 4:Correction improves class-conditional sample quality.We compare baseline (top) and correction (bottom), starting from the same noise in each column. Correction gives more coherent and detailed images for different classes and noises compared against the baseline.
Figure 5:Efficiency of correction training.FID converges within relatively few corrector training steps.

Figure 6:Iterative correction provides a controllable refinement trajectory on ImageNet.Left: Evolvement of the same samples over more correction steps. The main content remains the same while quality improves. Right: FID and precision–recall acrossKK. Correction gives a controllable tradeoff between coverage and quality and lower minimum FID.

Figure 7:Correction improvesunconditionalsample quality on ImageNet.Without correction, generated samples exhibit artifacts and structural inconsistencies (top), while corrective sampling produces diverse and high-quality images (bottom). The samples in each column share the same initial noise.
Figure 8:Correction lowers unconditional FID without guidance.50K training updates, 250 NFE, autoguidancew=7w=7.

Figure 10:Correction preserves more diversity and produces less oversaturation than CFG.Samples from SiTREPA-XL/2 with increasing correction depthKK(bottom) or CFG scaleww(top), at approximately matched NFE, same initial noise.

Figure 11:Correction improves object structure intext-to-imagegeneration.Compared with no correction (top), correction (bottom) separates the violin bodies, clarifies the guitar and car geometry, and organizes cluttered interiors. All samples are without CFG; full prompts are in AppendixB.3.

Figure 13:Correction improves the diversity of CFG samples while preserving quality.Columns compare no guidance (w=1w=1) and CFG (w=6w=6); rows compare no correction (K=0K=0) and correction (K=6K=6). All settings use the same eight seeds and number of denoising steps. Corrected samples show more varied bench shapes and viewpoints, with less oversaturation and a more natural appearance. Prompt: “a photo of a bench”.

Figure 15:Iterative correction sharpens predictions.We show the effect of iterative correction on JiT-L/16.(a)The base denoiser’s predictions (K=0K=0) are often incoherent and contain artifacts. Repeated correction resolves ambiguous structures and makes faces, object contours, and other details more coherent.(b)In extreme cases, correction appears to push this coherence too far, turning ambiguous structures in the base prediction into overly regular geometric shapes.
Further selected examples appear in AppendixD.2. Analytic target is computed using Eq.10in Appendix.

Figure 17:Measuring the training–inference gap with classifier two-sample tests.We train a classifier to distinguish samples from the training distribution and the inference distribution, and report AUROC and binary cross-entropy (BCE). Overall, correction makes classification harder, indicating a smaller gap between training and inference.

Figure 18:Correction beyond the supervised training depth improves generation (lower FID).Supervising more correction steps shifts the best-performing tested inference correction countKKtoward larger values, often approximately twice the maximum supervised depth. This suggests that “extrapolating” the learned correction beyond its training inputs may play an important role in the observed gains.
Figure 19:A frozen denoiser can support high quality refinement, but iterative correction can also oversaturate samples and produce abrupt changes in the sample prediction.
